Request reprint permissions here.During the boom years of the reform era, from 1978 to the early 2000s, China was a country of productive workers. The working-age population (those aged 15 to 64) rose from 57 percent of the population in 1978 to a peak of nearly 75 percent in 2010. They built the roads, factories, apartment complexes, and firms that powered three decades of close to ten percent annual growth—a 20-fold economic expansion.But over the past decade, this tide has turned. CARL MINZNER is a Senior Fellow for China Studies at the Council on Foreign Relations and a Professor at Fordham Law School. He is the author of the forthcoming book As China Ages: The Politics of Demographic Decline in the Counter-Reform Era, from which this essay is adapted. More by Carl Minzner
